items.q: `sealed class` vs `sealed interface` vs `enum` — when do you use each?
shortAnswer: `enum` is a fixed set of **singleton** constants, all the same shape. Each constant is one instance.
`sealed class` and `sealed interface` give a closed set of **types**. Each type can carry different data and have multiple instances.
`sealed interface` is the modern default: a type can implement several of them, so you can model overlapping categories that a sealed class hierarchy can't.
items.answer:
#### The distinction that matters
An `enum` constant is a single instance with fixed data — `Status.LOADING` is always the same object. A sealed subtype is a *type*: `Error(cause)` can have thousands of distinct instances carrying different payloads.

If the variants need to carry different data, you need sealed. If they're just labels, `enum` is lighter and gives you `values()`, `entries`, `valueOf`, and `ordinal` for free.

#### Exhaustiveness
Both give the compiler a closed set, so `when` is exhaustive without an `else`. **Always omit the `else`** — add a variant and it becomes a compile error at every site that must handle it; `else` throws that safety away. Kotlin 2.3 made exhaustiveness data-flow-aware.

#### Why sealed interface is usually better
- A class can implement **multiple** sealed interfaces, modeling cross-cutting categories — an error that is both `Retryable` and `UserFacing`.
- No forced inheritance relationship, so implementations stay free to extend something else.
- Existing types can join the hierarchy.

`sealed class` is still right when the variants genuinely share state or behaviour that belongs in a base class.

#### Sealed + data object
`data object Loading : UiState` gives a proper `toString()` — `Loading` rather than the object default with a hash — which matters in logs and test failures.

#### Permitted subtypes
Subtypes must live in the same package and module (previously the same file). That's what makes the set closed and the check sound.

code.caption: Overlapping categories that a sealed class can't express

followUps: Why is omitting `else` on a sealed `when` a feature rather than an oversight?
When would you still prefer an enum over a sealed interface?
How do sealed hierarchies interact with `kotlinx.serialization` polymorphism?
traps: Adding `else -> {}` to a sealed `when`. You've just disabled the compiler check that makes sealed types worth using.
Using an enum for states that need to carry data, then bolting on a nullable payload field that's only valid for some constants.

items.q: How are extension functions resolved? Why does that surprise people?
shortAnswer: Extensions are **statically dispatched**: the compiler picks them from the receiver's *declared* type, not the runtime type.
They compile to static methods with the receiver as the first parameter. They don't modify the class and can't be overridden.
A member function always wins over an extension with the same signature. The extension silently becomes unreachable.
items.answer:
#### Static dispatch
Take `open class Base` / `class Derived : Base()` with `fun Base.name() = "Base"` and `fun Derived.name() = "Derived"` — then `val x: Base = Derived(); x.name()` resolves to `"Base"`, because the pick comes from the **declared** type.

That's the surprise: member functions are virtual and an extension looks identical at the call site. Extensions are sugar over `NameKt.name(x)`.

#### Members win
If a class has a member with the same name and signature, the member is always called. Add a member later and every call site silently switches behaviour — no warning, no error. Real hazard when you extend a class you don't control.

#### What they compile to
`fun String.shout(): String = uppercase() + "!"` becomes `public static String shout(String $receiver)`. From Java: `UtilsKt.shout("hi")`. Use `@JvmName` on the file to give that generated class a decent name.

#### Where they earn their keep in Android
- Adding domain-specific helpers to framework classes you can't modify (`Context.dp`, `View.hide()`).
- Keeping mapping logic out of data classes: `UserDto.toDomain()` lives next to the code that cares, not on the DTO.
- Scoped DSLs via extension *lambdas* (`build.gradle.kts`, Compose modifiers, `buildString`).

#### Extension properties
Same rules; note they can't hold state — there's no backing field, only a getter. `val View.isVisible get() = visibility == VISIBLE`.

#### Nullable receivers
`fun String?.orEmpty()` is legal — the receiver can be null inside the body. That's how the stdlib provides null-safe helpers.

code.caption: Static dispatch in action, and the member-wins trap

followUps: How would you call a Kotlin extension function from Java?
Why can't extension properties have backing fields?
How do extension lambdas (`T.() -> Unit`) enable type-safe builders?
traps: Assuming extensions are polymorphic. This is the single most common Kotlin trick question.
Writing an extension for a class you don't own, then breaking silently when the library adds a member with that name.

items.q: What's new in Kotlin 2.x that you use day to day?
shortAnswer: **K2** is the compiler. It's faster, has one frontend across platforms, and gives much better type inference and error messages.
Kotlin **2.3** stabilized nested type aliases, explicit backing fields, an unused-return-value checker, and data-flow `when` exhaustiveness. **2.4** is the current release (Jun 2026).
What you notice on Android: better inference, faster builds, and `expect`/`actual` plus Swift export maturing for KMP.
items.answer:
#### K2
The rewritten compiler frontend. What you notice:
- Materially faster compilation, especially on large codebases.
- Smarter smart-casts and inference, so code that used to need explicit types now compiles.
- Clearer diagnostics.
- One frontend for JVM/Native/JS/Wasm, which is why KMP features now land uniformly.

#### Kotlin 2.3 highlights
- **Explicit backing fields** — `val flow: StateFlow<T> field = MutableStateFlow(...)`. This kills the `_state`/`state` boilerplate pair every ViewModel has been writing: one property, private mutable type inside, public read-only type outside.
- **Nested type aliases** — `typealias` can now be declared inside a class, so an alias is scoped where it is meaningful.
- **Unused return value checker** — flags calls whose result you discarded but shouldn't have, catching the `list.filter { }`-with-no-assignment bug class.
- **Data-flow-based `when` exhaustiveness** — the compiler proves more `when` expressions complete.
- Stable time-tracking APIs and improved `Uuid` in the stdlib.

#### Kotlin 2.4 (Jun 2026)
The current stable line (2.3.20 added name-based destructuring and an immutable-copy API for `Map.Entry`). Verify the current number against the release notes.

#### Context parameters
The successor to experimental context receivers — ambient dependencies (a logger, a transaction, a scope) without threading them through every signature. Check its stability level before relying on it.

#### How to answer this well
Don't recite a changelog. Pick the one or two that changed how you write code — for most Android developers that's **explicit backing fields** and **K2 build speed** — and say what they replaced.

code.caption: Explicit backing fields vs. the boilerplate they replace

followUps: What problem do context parameters solve that plain parameters don't?
How did K2 change smart-cast behaviour you might rely on?
What's the migration risk when moving a large codebase to a new Kotlin major?
traps: Naming features you haven't used. Interviewers follow up with 'where did you apply that?' and vagueness is worse than not mentioning it.
Confusing context parameters with the older experimental context receivers — they're different designs.

items.q: How do you model errors in Kotlin? Exceptions, `Result`, or a sealed type?
shortAnswer: Kotlin has **no checked exceptions**, so the type system says nothing about what can fail. That's why explicit error modeling matters more than in Java.
Use a **sealed result type** for expected, recoverable domain failures the UI must render differently. Use **exceptions** for programming errors and truly exceptional conditions.
`kotlin.Result` is fine internally but awkward as a public API type. And `runCatching` catches `CancellationException`, which silently breaks coroutine cancellation.
items.answer:
#### The problem
Java's checked exceptions were widely disliked, but they did document failure. Kotlin removed them, so `fun load(): User` gives you no hint that it throws. Left alone, this produces apps that crash on a `SocketTimeoutException` nobody anticipated.

#### Three tools, three jobs
**Exceptions** — for bugs and unrecoverable conditions: `IllegalStateException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `require`/`check`/`error`. These should crash in debug and be reported in release; don't catch them broadly.

**Sealed result types** — for expected domain failures. The UI genuinely needs to distinguish "no network", "not found", "rate limited", and "invalid input" because each renders differently. Encode that in the type so `when` forces you to handle each.

**`kotlin.Result<T>`** — a built-in success/failure wrapper. Useful inside a layer, but: it can only carry a `Throwable`, it has restrictions as a return type in some positions, and it doesn't express *which* failures are possible. Most codebases end up with their own sealed type.

#### The runCatching trap
`runCatching { repo.load() }` also catches `CancellationException`. When a coroutine is cancelled, `CancellationException` is thrown at the suspension point as normal control flow. Swallowing it means the coroutine keeps running after cancellation — structured concurrency quietly stops working. Either use explicit `catch` clauses for the types you expect, or rethrow cancellation.

#### Where to convert
Convert at the **data layer boundary**: the repository catches `IOException`/`HttpException` and returns your domain error type. Above that line, no code deals in Retrofit or SQLite exceptions, keeping domain and UI layers free of transport concerns and trivially testable.

code.caption: Domain error type, safe conversion, and exhaustive UI handling

followUps: Why exactly does `runCatching` break coroutine cancellation?
When is `kotlin.Result` the right choice over a custom sealed type?
Where in the architecture should transport exceptions be converted, and why there?
traps: `catch (e: Exception)` around suspending code. `CancellationException` is an `Exception`, so you break cancellation without noticing.
Letting Retrofit's `HttpException` leak into ViewModels and composables — now your UI layer depends on your HTTP client.

items.q: How do type-safe builders and DSLs work? Where do you meet them in Android?
shortAnswer: The mechanism is a **lambda with receiver**: `T.() -> Unit`. Inside the lambda, `this` is a `T`, so members are in scope without a qualifier.
That's why `build.gradle.kts`, `buildString`, Compose `Modifier` chains, and Kotlin serialization config all read like small languages.
`@DslMarker` blocks implicit access to outer receivers. That's what stops nesting bugs in nested builders.
items.answer:
#### The core trick
`fun html(block: HtmlBuilder.() -> Unit): Html { val builder = HtmlBuilder(); builder.block(); return builder.build() }` — `this` inside the lambda IS the builder. Because the lambda's receiver is the builder, calling `body { }` inside resolves against the builder without any qualifier. Combined with the trailing-lambda syntax (`html { … }`), you get something that reads like declarative markup but is fully type-checked and IDE-completable.

#### The @DslMarker problem
With nested builders, the inner lambda can still see the *outer* receiver's members, so `html { body { head { } } }` compiles when it shouldn't — `head` belongs to the outer html scope. Annotate your builder types with a `@DslMarker` annotation and the compiler forbids implicit access to outer receivers. Every serious DSL does this.

#### Where you already use it
- **Gradle Kotlin DSL** — `android { defaultConfig { … } }` is exactly this pattern.
- **`buildString`, `buildList`, `buildMap`** in the stdlib.
- **Compose** — `LazyColumn { item { } items() { } }` is a builder DSL; `Modifier` is a chained builder.
- **kotlinx.serialization** `Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }`.
- **OkHttp/Retrofit** builders (Java-style, but the Kotlin extensions add DSL wrappers).
- **`Room`/`WorkManager`** request builders.

#### When to build your own
A DSL is worth it when a configuration is genuinely nested and will be written many times — test fixtures, navigation graphs, complex UI configuration. It is *not* worth it for a data class with four fields; named arguments and default values already solve that in Kotlin, which is why the Builder pattern is much rarer here than in Java.

code.caption: A small DSL with @DslMarker, and the test-fixture use case

followUps: Why does Kotlin rarely need the Builder pattern compared to Java?
How does `apply` relate to lambdas with receiver?
traps: Building a DSL where named arguments would do. Extra machinery for no readability gain reads as over-engineering.
Omitting `@DslMarker` and shipping a DSL where nested scopes silently accept the wrong calls.
